note: From the 2026-08-03 research pass. Leads failed only our evidence bar or the count; blocked can never ship.

leads.name: Milestone Hackberry of the Todai-ji West Gate
leads.why: 3.95m girth and 30m, the tallest tree in the official Nara Park giant-tree course, believed to mark the milestone on the Kyoto road that begins at Todai-ji's Tegai-mon. Age explicitly not recorded, single official source, and no coordinate exists for the West Gate ruins in any gazetteer. Needs a pin before it can ship. CHECKED AGAIN 2026-08-14 (verify pass): confirmed the source is the Ministry of the Environment's own giant-tree database (kyoju.biodic.go.jp, both the illustrated English course PDF at kyoju.biodic.go.jp/files/course/001/guide_narakouen_en.pdf and the Japanese course page, _command=modelCourse001), an official government register, so it counts as one source. Could NOT find an independent second source: several WebSearch summaries claimed a prefectural natural monument designation, but a direct fetch of Nara City's own designated-monument list (city.nara.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/2460.html) does NOT include this tree, so that designation claim does not hold up and must not be repeated. No blog, society survey (checked kyoboku.jp's Nara Park page) or second register turned it up. The historical Todaiji West Gate ruin site itself has a documented address (406-1 Zoshi-cho, same as the temple generally) but no tree-level coordinate. Still needs: one more independent source for existence/species, and a coordinate (satellite/aerial identification of the ruin mound, which the government PDF's course map places just west of Todaiji-nandaimon Gate near Mitoriiike pond, between Isuien Garden and the Nara Prefectural Museum).

leads.name: Roben-sugi at Nigatsu-do [RESOLVED 2026-08-14, delivered as nra_010]
leads.why: Superb legend: the infant Roben was said to have been carried off by an eagle and left in its branches, and Todai-ji's founding abbot was reunited with his mother beneath it. Confirmed 2026-08-14 across four independent sources (jinja-tera-gosyuin-meguri.com, naratrip.com, gururinkansai.com, data.japanmystery.com): the original tree lived roughly 600 years and stood ~21.2m before the Second Muroto Typhoon destroyed it on 16 September 1961; sources disagree on the exact generation count since (third vs fourth planting) but agree the present tree is a replanting roughly six decades old. Delivered to data/research/nara-verified.json as nra_010, location_precision approximate (shrine-level: below the Nigatsu-do slope, north of Kojo Shrine), story must say plainly it is a replanting.

leads.name: Wakamiya Great Camphor, Kasuga Taisha
leads.why: Legend says Empress Jingu planted it. Sources contradict badly on size: 12.46m girth and 24m in one record against '8m+, 7m tall, three trees planted together' in another, which is not a rounding difference. No official register lists it, and the one open photo fails the card crop with stone lanterns filling the centre. CHECKED AGAIN 2026-08-14 (verify pass): a WebSearch summary surfaced a THIRD figure, 11.46m girth and 24m height, calling it 'one of the top 1-2 largest trees in Nara Prefecture' and giving the alternate name 'Chitose Kusu' (千歳楠); could not trace this to a specific fetchable page to confirm it independently, and it does not resolve the existing conflict, it deepens it (three different girths now: 12.46m, 11.46m, and 8m+). Also confirmed via direct fetch of narashikanko.or.jp and kasugataisha.or.jp/en pages that the well-documented '8.7m girth, 25m, 800-1000 years' figure circulating in search results belongs to the Great Cedar (Shato-no-Ohsugi, already published as nra_002), not this camphor; that mix-up is why the size kept looking resolvable and wasn't. Do not ship until a single fetchable, citable source can be pinned down for one girth figure; this is now a three-way conflict, not two-way.

leads.name: Great Zelkova of Kasuga
leads.why: 4.9m girth, the largest zelkova in Nara Park, hollow and mossy. Single-sourced to the shrine's own forest-walk page, no coordinate, no age, and 'upper portions lost' needs checking that it is thriving rather than a relic.

leads.name: Yogo-no-Matsu, Kasuga Taisha
leads.why: NEVER SHIP. The original pine died in 1995; a successor sapling grows beside the surviving stump. Famous as the claimed origin of the pine painted on every Noh stage, though even that attribution is disputed as a later invention.

leads.name: Chisokuin Nara-no-Yaezakura
leads.why: NEVER SHIP. The tree designated a national Natural Monument in 1923 has died; today's cherries are propagated descendants. Chisokuin is a closed sub-temple open roughly one day a year.

leads.name: Kasugayama Primeval Forest
leads.why: NEVER SHIP as one entry. A Special Natural Monument covering a whole mountain, with no single tree and nowhere to stand. A named individual inside it can qualify separately.

leads.name: The Cedar of the Shrine Path near Nigatsu-do
leads.why: RETIRED 2026-09-08, one day after publication. Published from a reader's photograph with ZERO verified sources, against the standing bar of two independent sources for existence, species and age. The run applied 'publish and ask' (2026-08-13), which covers an empty FIELD on a tree that clears the bar, not the question of whether the tree clears it at all. Each story argued against its own inclusion: the Nigatsu-do slope 'holds cedars like this by the dozen', the pond could not be named, the temple behind the wall could not be established. Nothing here is wrong about the trees; they are simply not established as remarkable, which is what a city page promises. Everything is kept: the photograph, the coordinate and the full story. Goes back the day a source names one.
leads.story:
Ninety-nine metres from Nigatsu-do's famous Roben-sugi stands a second cedar nobody has named. A reader photographed it beside a small shrine building on the same forested slope, in the cluster of guardian sub-shrines, Kojo-sha, Iimichi-jinja and Onyu-jinja among them, that share this stretch of Todai-ji's outer precinct.

The trunk is buttressed and straight, old enough to belong here rather than beside it, and its crown forks the way a cedar's does once it has stopped competing for height with the pines around it. The old-growth forest around Nigatsu-do holds cedars like this by the dozen, most with no individual record at all: land this old accumulates trees faster than anyone can catalogue them.

We could not match this one to any of the three named sub-shrines, or find a register entry for a cedar at this exact spot, so nothing here has an age or a girth. What we have is a photograph, a coordinate and a species that is not in doubt.

If you know which shrine this stands beside, or have stood in front of it yourself, tell us. Todai-ji's precinct is free and open, the same ground as the Roben-sugi a short walk away.
leads.access: Free, open ground within Todai-ji's outer Nigatsu-do precinct, the same forested slope as the Roben-sugi

leads.story:
This cedar leans hard over the gravel road climbing toward Nigatsu-do, close enough to the power lines strung across it that whoever put them up clearly decided the tree was staying. A reader's photograph is the only record of it: no register, no temple page, no name.

Todai-ji's Nigatsu-do hillside is old forest rather than a planted garden, and it holds cedars like this in numbers nobody has individually catalogued, unlike the Roben-sugi eighty-nine metres away, which earned its name from a legend rather than its age. This one has no legend attached, just a lean pronounced enough to notice from the road and a trunk old enough to have outlasted whatever once grew beside it and left it leaning that way.

Species is certain from the bark and foliage in the photograph. Age, girth and name are not recorded anywhere we could find in the time we had to look.

The whole hillside is open, free ground, part of Todai-ji's outer precinct. If you know this tree by name, or can say why it leans the way it does, we would like to hear it.
leads.access: Free, open ground beside a gravel road within Todai-ji's outer precinct

leads.story:
A reader's photograph places a broad, dense-crowned tree beside a wooden rest pavilion and a small pond somewhere in the open ground between Todai-ji and Kasuga Taisha, part of Nara Park's Kasugano stretch. Several ponds sit in this area, Kagami-ike among the named ones, and none lines up exactly with the coordinate the phone recorded, so this entry cannot say which one.

The crown shape and leaf density suggest a mature zelkova, one of the more common large park trees in Nara, but the photograph does not show the bark or leaf edges clearly enough to be sure, so the species stays a guess rather than a claim.

What is certain is that a real tree stands there: broad-canopied, mature, shading a pavilion that people clearly use to rest. Nara Park carries no fences or opening hours across this whole stretch, so whatever it turns out to be, anyone can walk up to it today.

If you know this spot, the name of the pond or the pavilion would place it precisely, and the species would settle the rest.
leads.access: Free, open parkland; this stretch of Nara Park between Todai-ji and Kasuga Taisha has no fences or opening hours

leads.story:
A ginkgo with a heavily fluted, multi-stemmed base grows beside a long plastered wall with the tiled coping of a temple precinct, on a small street of shops and houses a few minutes walk from Todai-ji's southern approach. A second ginkgo of the same size stands further along the same wall in the reader's photograph, which is the only record either tree has.

Ginkgo is not in doubt from the fan-shaped leaves, but which temple the wall belongs to is: nothing we could find names a great ginkgo on this street, and the shopfronts around it carry no sign of what lies behind the wall. Whatever the answer, the tree itself stands in view from the pavement, which is where the photograph was taken.

Age, girth and the temple's name are all missing from this entry, which is unusual for a tree this size and this obviously old. If you know this street, a few hundred metres north of Kofuku-ji in Nara, the missing name is probably one sentence away.
leads.access: Visible from the public street; which temple's grounds lie behind the wall is not established
